units.title: Early Ultrasound Signs & Biometry Dating
units.guide: Early transvaginal sonography identifies sequential gestational hallmarks: the intradecidual sign representing interstitial blastocyst burrowing, the double decidual sign confirming intrauterine pregnancy, and the double bleb sign pairing yolk and amniotic sacs. Crown-rump length (CRL) serves as the gold standard parameter for dating up to 13 weeks + 6 days.

units.title: Second Trimester Biometry, Cervical Length & Fetal Echo
units.guide: Beyond 14 weeks, fetal biometry relies on biparietal diameter (BPD, measured outer-to-inner in the transthalamic plane), head circumference, abdominal circumference (AC, single best growth marker), and femur length. Transvaginal cervical length screening identifies preterm birth risk (<25 mm), while specialized fetal echocardiography at 22-24 weeks evaluates cardiac anomalies.

units.title: Anomaly Scan (TIFFA) & Cranial NTDs: Anencephaly & Acrania
units.sec: Level II scan & cranial defects · p330-331
units.guide: Targeted Imaging for Fetal Anomalies (TIFFA / Level 2 scan) is universally performed between 18 and 22 weeks. Failure of anterior neuropore closure yields acrania and anencephaly, marked by absent calvarium, deep shallow orbits ('frog-eye' or 'Mickey Mouse' appearance), absent fetal adrenals causing post-term gestation, and polyhydramnios.

units.title: Spina Bifida, Arnold-Chiari II Signs & Craniorachischisis
units.guide: Spina bifida results from failure of caudal vertebral arches to close, ranging from spina bifida occulta to open meningomyelocele. Classic sonographic hallmarks of Chiari II malformation include the 'lemon sign' (scalloped frontal bones), 'banana sign' (downward displaced cerebellum obliterating the cisterna magna), and hydrocephalus.

units.title: Abdominal Wall Defects: Omphalocele vs Gastroschisis
units.guide: Omphalocele is a midline umbilical defect enclosed within an amnioperitoneal sac with the umbilical cord inserting onto its apex, carrying high aneuploidy risks. Gastroschisis is a right paraumbilical defect with bowel loops floating freely in amniotic fluid without a membrane, exhibiting normal cord insertion and marked AFP elevation.

units.title: Alpha-Fetoprotein (AFP) Biology & Diagnostic Deviations
units.guide: Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP), synthesized by the fetal yolk sac, liver, and gut, is evaluated between 15 and 20 weeks. Elevated MSAFP signifies open NTDs, abdominal wall defects, or multiple gestations, whereas decreased MSAFP is seen in fetal aneuploidies, maternal diabetes, and gestational trophoblastic disease ('Diabetic GOAT').

units.title: Aneuploidy Principles & Down Syndrome Genetics
units.guide: Aneuploidies stem from chromosomal non-disjunction, Robertsonian translocations, or mosaicism, with Trisomy 16 being the most common cause of early miscarriage. Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) is the most viable autosomal trisomy, carrying a 100% recurrence risk if a parent harbors a balanced t(21;21) Robertsonian translocation.

units.title: First Trimester Screening: Dual Test & Combined Test
units.guide: First trimester screening at 11w0d to 13w6d (CRL 45-84 mm) combines biochemical analytes and sonography. The Dual test measures PAPP-A (decreased) and free beta-hCG (increased in Down syndrome). Combining the Dual test with nuchal translucency (Combined test) achieves an 85-87% detection rate.

units.title: Nuchal Translucency & Cystic Hygroma Differentiation
units.guide: Nuchal translucency (NT) is measured in the mid-sagittal plane with a neutral fetal head, considered abnormal when >=3 mm. Increased NT associates with Down syndrome, Turner syndrome, and congenital heart defects. Cystic hygroma is a larger, multiseptated posterior neck lymphangioma with a very high predictive value for aneuploidy.

units.title: Second Trimester Markers: Triple, Quad & Soft Sonographic Signs
units.guide: Second trimester biochemical screening between 15 and 20 weeks comprises the Triple test and Quad test (adding Inhibin-A). Down syndrome exhibits high hCG and Inhibin-A with low AFP and uE3 ('HI' is high). Key sonographic soft markers include thickened nuchal fold (>=6 mm), absent nasal bone, echogenic intracardiac focus, and choroid plexus cysts.

units.title: Non-Invasive Prenatal Testing (NIPT / cffDNA) & Integrated Screening
units.guide: NIPT analyzes cell-free fetal DNA derived from apoptotic syncytiotrophoblasts in maternal plasma from 10 weeks onward, offering >99% sensitivity for Trisomy 21. Integrated screening fuses first-trimester Combined testing with second-trimester Quad screening to achieve 85-95% detection rates while minimizing invasive procedures.

units.title: Aneuploidy Risk Interpretation & Diagnostic Algorithm
units.guide: Screening results are expressed as personalized risk ratios, using established cutoffs of 1:250 for Down syndrome and 1:100 for Trisomies 18 and 13. Screen-positive findings prompt counseling for secondary screening via NIPT or definitive invasive diagnostic confirmation via CVS (T1) or amniocentesis (T2).

questions.q: On early transvaginal sonography, the 'intradecidual sign' represents which fundamental embryological event?
opts: Interstitial implantation of the blastocyst within the thickened endometrium
Complete separation of the amnion and chorion
Decidual capsularis stretching over the developing embryo
Appearance of the secondary yolk sac
questions.exp: The intradecidual sign is the first sonographic sign of pregnancy, reflecting interstitial implantation of the blastocyst within the decidua. (Book p327)

questions.q: The 'double decidual sac sign' (double ring sign) on transvaginal ultrasound confirms an intrauterine pregnancy. What anatomical layers form the inner and outer rings?
opts: Inner ring: Decidua capsularis; Outer ring: Decidua parietalis
Inner ring: Decidua basalis; Outer ring: Decidua capsularis
Inner ring: Amnion; Outer ring: Chorion laeve
Inner ring: Decidua parietalis; Outer ring: Myometrium
questions.exp: The double decidual ring consists of an inner ring (decidua capsularis) and an outer ring (decidua parietalis), confirming intrauterine pregnancy. (Book p327)

questions.q: The 'double bleb sign' observed on early first-trimester TVS consists of the simultaneous visualization of which two adjacent fluid cavities?
opts: The yolk sac and the developing amniotic sac
The gestational sac and the pseudogestational sac
The right and left lateral cerebral ventricles
The vitelline duct and the allantois
questions.exp: The double bleb sign represents the transient side-by-side appearance of the secondary yolk sac and the expanding amniotic sac with the embryonic disc between them. (Book p327)

questions.q: What is the single most accurate ultrasound parameter for determining gestational age across the entire pregnancy?
opts: Crown-Rump Length (CRL) measured in the first trimester
Biparietal diameter (BPD) measured at 18 weeks
Femur length (FL) measured in the second trimester
Abdominal circumference (AC) measured in the third trimester
questions.exp: Crown-rump length (CRL) measured between 7 and 9 weeks (usable up to 13w6d) is the single most accurate parameter for pregnancy dating (+/- 3-5 days). (Book p327)

questions.q: Before an embryonic fetal pole is clearly measurable, the Mean Sac Diameter (MSD) can estimate gestational age in days using which formula?
opts: Gestational age (in days) = MSD (in mm) + 30
Gestational age (in days) = MSD (in mm) + 42
Gestational age (in days) = MSD (in mm) x 7
Gestational age (in days) = MSD (in mm) + 14
questions.exp: Gestational age in days can be estimated from early sac dimensions using: MSD (in mm) + 30 = gestational age in days. (Book p328)

questions.q: Crown-Rump Length (CRL) is valid for gestational age estimation up to 13 weeks + 6 days, provided the CRL measurement remains below:
opts: 84 mm
65 mm
100 mm
50 mm
questions.exp: CRL is used up to 13 weeks + 6 days and CRL < 84 mm; once CRL >= 84 mm, biparietal diameter (BPD) and head circumference are utilized. (Book p328)

questions.q: In a twin gestation conceived spontaneously where a size discrepancy exists between the two fetuses on first-trimester ultrasound, the EDD is determined by:
opts: The CRL measurement of the larger twin
The CRL measurement of the smaller twin
The mathematical average of both CRL measurements
Discarding the ultrasound and relying strictly on LMP
questions.exp: In twin pregnancies with growth discrepancy, gestational age dating and EDD calculation are based on the larger fetus to avoid missing early growth restriction. (Book p328)

questions.q: When measuring the Biparietal Diameter (BPD) in the second trimester, the ultrasound calipers should be placed on which anatomical skull margins?
opts: From the outer table of the proximal parietal bone to the inner table of the distal parietal bone
From the outer table to the outer table of both parietal bones
From the inner table to the inner table of both parietal bones
Across the fronto-occipital axis
questions.exp: BPD is measured in the transthalamic plane from the outer table of the skull on the near field to the inner table of the skull on the far field. (Book p328)

questions.q: Which fetal biometric parameter is considered the single most sensitive marker for assessing fetal nutritional status, IUGR, and macrosomia?
opts: Abdominal Circumference (AC)
Biparietal Diameter (BPD)
Femur Length (FL)
Head Circumference (HC)
questions.exp: Abdominal circumference reflects fetal liver size and subcutaneous abdominal fat stores, making it the most sensitive biometry parameter for fetal growth. (Book p328)

questions.q: What is the recommended gestational window for conducting the routine Targeted Imaging for Fetal Anomalies (TIFFA / Level II scan)?
opts: 18 to 22 weeks of gestation
11 to 13 weeks + 6 days
24 to 28 weeks of gestation
32 to 34 weeks of gestation
questions.exp: The Level II anomaly scan (TIFFA) is universally recommended for all pregnant women between 18 and 22 weeks of gestation. (Book p328)

questions.q: In women with a history of spontaneous preterm birth, transvaginal cervical length screening is indicated; a cervical length is considered abnormal when it measures:
opts: < 25 mm before 24 weeks of gestation
< 35 mm at 28 weeks
< 15 mm at 36 weeks
< 40 mm in the first trimester
questions.exp: A TVS cervical length < 25 mm prior to 24 weeks identifies high risk for recurrent preterm labor and is an indication for vaginal progesterone or cerclage. (Book p329)

questions.q: What is the optimal gestational age to assess definitive placental localization to diagnose or exclude placenta previa, and when should borderline cases be repeated?
opts: Best evaluated at 32 weeks, and repeated at 36 weeks
Evaluated at 12 weeks, repeated at 18 weeks
Evaluated at 20 weeks, repeated at 24 weeks
Evaluated at 38 weeks only
questions.exp: Placental localization is best assessed at 32 weeks (accounting for trophotropism/apparent placental migration) and confirmed at 36 weeks if low-lying. (Book p329)

questions.q: A specialized fetal echocardiogram is ideally performed between 22 and 24 weeks of gestation. Which of the following is a recognized maternal indication?
opts: First-trimester lithium exposure (risk of Ebstein anomaly)
Controlled gestational hypertension on labetalol
Maternal iron deficiency anemia
History of uncomplicated twin delivery
questions.exp: Indications for fetal echo include lithium exposure (Ebstein anomaly), maternal anti-Ro/SSA antibodies (congenital heart block), maternal pregestational DM, and aneuploidy. (Book p329)

questions.q: What is the fundamental embryological defect underlying anencephaly?
opts: Failure of closure of the cranial (anterior) neuropore around day 24-26
Failure of closure of the caudal (posterior) neuropore around day 26-28
Premature fusion of the sagittal cranial suture
Agenesis of the corpus callosum
questions.exp: Anencephaly results from failure of closure of the cranial neuropore, leaving neuroectoderm exposed to amniotic fluid where it degenerates. (Book p330)

questions.q: What is the most frequent anatomical site for the development of a fetal encephalocele?
opts: Occipital bone (75-80%)
Frontal bone
Parietal bone
Sphenoid bone
questions.exp: Encephaloceles most commonly arise in the occipital region through a calvarial defect in the occipital bone. (Book p330)

questions.q: Anencephaly is characteristically associated with post-term pregnancy (>42 weeks). What is the underlying pathophysiological mechanism?
opts: Absence or hypoplasia of fetal pituitary and adrenal glands leading to deficient DHEAS and reduced estrogen
Excessive production of fetal progesterone by the placenta
Premature rupture of membranes
Severe maternal hyperprolactinemia
questions.exp: Anencephalic fetuses lack hypothalamus/pituitary-adrenal stimulation, leading to deficient DHEAS, low maternal estrogen, and failure of labor initiation. (Book p331)

questions.q: Why is polyhydramnios frequently seen in fetuses affected by anencephaly during the late second and third trimesters?
opts: Impaired fetal swallowing reflex combined with transudation of fluid from exposed neural tissue
Excessive fetal urination secondary to renal hypertrophy
Severe fetal cardiac failure causing polyuria
Overproduction of lung surfactant into amniotic fluid
questions.exp: Polyhydramnios develops because the anencephalic fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid due to lack of cerebral swallowing centers. (Book p331)

questions.q: What is the earliest gestational age at which anencephaly can be recognized on transvaginal sonography, and what is the classic facial sign?
opts: Earliest at 10-12 weeks; 'Frog-eye' or 'Mickey Mouse' sign due to prominent bulging orbits and absent calvarium
Earliest at 18 weeks; 'Lemon sign'
Earliest at 24 weeks; 'Banana sign'
Earliest at 6 weeks; 'Double bleb sign'
questions.exp: Anencephaly can be spotted at 10-12 weeks (best at 14w) displaying the 'frog-eye' or 'Mickey Mouse' appearance of prominent globes with absent skull vault. (Book p331)

questions.q: What is the empiric recurrence risk of a neural tube defect in a subsequent pregnancy after ONE previously affected child?
opts: Approximately 3% to 5%
Approximately 0.1%
Approximately 25%
Approximately 50%
questions.exp: The recurrence risk of an NTD is approximately 3-5% after one affected pregnancy, rising to 10% after two affected pregnancies. (Book p331)

questions.q: Maternal hyperthermia or fever (body temperature elevated by >= 1.5°C) during the first trimester is recognized as a teratogenic risk factor for:
opts: Neural tube defects, microcephaly, and neurodevelopmental delay
Omphalocele and gastroschisis
Renal agenesis (Potter sequence)
Skeletal dysplasias
questions.exp: First-trimester hyperthermia/fever (elevated >=1.5°C) disrupts mitotic neurogenesis and neuropore closure, causing NTDs and microcephaly. (Book p332)

questions.q: What is considered the gold-standard, most sensitive biochemical marker measured in amniotic fluid to confirm an open neural tube defect?
opts: Acetylcholinesterase (AChE)
Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)
Unconjugated estriol (uE3)
Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
questions.exp: Amniotic fluid acetylcholinesterase (AChE) is the best, highly specific biochemical marker for open neural tube defects. (Book p332)

questions.q: In spina bifida aperta, what is the anatomical difference between a meningocele and a meningomyelocele?
opts: Meningocele involves herniation of meninges only; meningomyelocele involves herniation of both meninges and spinal cord elements
Meningocele is covered by intact skin; meningomyelocele is completely open
Meningocele contains brain tissue; meningomyelocele contains spinal cord
Meningocele occurs only in the occiput; meningomyelocele occurs only in the sacrum
questions.exp: A meningocele contains only meninges and cerebrospinal fluid in the herniated sac; a meningomyelocele contains neural tissue/spinal cord as well. (Book p332)

questions.q: On cranial ultrasound of a fetus with open spina bifida, the 'Banana sign' refers to:
opts: Anterior curvature and caudal displacement of the cerebellum around the brainstem, obliterating the cisterna magna
Scalloping and inward indentation of the frontal cranial bones
Severe asymmetrical dilation of the lateral ventricles
Absence of the cavum septum pellucidum
questions.exp: The 'banana sign' describes the cerebellar vermis herniating into the foramen magnum and curving anteriorly around the brainstem in Arnold-Chiari II malformation. (Book p332)

questions.q: The 'Lemon sign' seen on second-trimester fetal cranial sonography is characterized by:
opts: Inward scalloping and concavity of the frontal calvarial bones due to reduced intracranial pressure
A narrow, elongated anterior fontanelle
Widening of the posterior fossa cistern
Bulging parietal bones with coronal synostosis
questions.exp: The 'lemon sign' represents inward scalloping of the frontal bones produced by downward traction on intracranial contents in open spina bifida. (Book p332)

questions.q: The severe lethal malformation termed 'Craniorachischisis' is characterized by:
opts: Combined continuous failure of neural tube closure encompassing both anencephaly and total open spina bifida
Occipital encephalocele accompanied by polycystic kidneys
Herniation of the posterior fossa contents into an occipital sac (Chiari III)
Isolated sacrococcygeal teratoma with open spine
questions.exp: Craniorachischisis is the most extreme form of NTD, with complete non-closure of the neural tube extending from the brainstem throughout the entire spine. (Book p333)

questions.q: What is the critical anatomical covering that distinguishes an omphalocele from gastroschisis?
opts: An omphalocele is enclosed within a protective peritoneal-amniotic sac; gastroschisis is completely uncovered
Gastroschisis is enclosed within a thick amnion sac; omphalocele is uncovered
Both defects are always enclosed within Wharton's jelly
Both defects lack any peritoneal covering
questions.exp: An omphalocele is enclosed by a two-layered sac (peritoneum internally, amnion externally); gastroschisis is an open defect without any covering sac. (Book p333)

questions.q: Where is the abdominal wall defect located in gastroschisis relative to the umbilical cord insertion?
opts: Full-thickness defect located to the right of a normally inserted umbilical cord
Directly through the midline umbilical ring
Full-thickness defect to the left of the umbilical cord
Supraumbilical midline defect involving the lower sternum
questions.exp: Gastroschisis is located almost always immediately to the right of an intact, normally attached umbilical cord. (Book p334)

questions.q: In which anterior abdominal wall defect is the insertion of the umbilical cord situated directly onto the apex of the herniated sac?
opts: Omphalocele
Gastroschisis
Bladder exstrophy
Prune belly syndrome
questions.exp: In omphalocele, the umbilical cord inserts directly onto the apex of the membranous sac, with umbilical vessels radiating across its surface. (Book p334)

questions.q: Which abdominal wall defect carries a very high rate of associated chromosomal aneuploidies (particularly Trisomy 18 and 13) and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome?
opts: Omphalocele (50-70% associated anomalies; karyotyping indicated)
Gastroschisis (aneuploidy is extremely rare; karyotyping not routinely indicated)
Urachal fistula
Patent vitelline duct
questions.exp: Omphalocele is associated with major chromosomal trisomies (Trisomy 18 > 13 > 21) and syndromes in >50% of cases, warranting karyotyping. (Book p334)

questions.q: Why must a definitive sonographic diagnosis of omphalocele NEVER be made before 11 completed weeks of gestation?
opts: Because physiological midgut herniation into the umbilical cord normally persists until 9-11 weeks
Because the liver does not develop until 12 weeks
Because amniotic fluid volume is insufficient for visualization
Because fetal abdominal muscles do not form until the second trimester
questions.exp: Physiological midgut rotation and herniation into the umbilical coelom is normal between 6 and 10 weeks; diagnosis of omphalocele is made after 11 weeks. (Book p334)

questions.q: During human fetal development, alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is predominantly synthesized by which tissues?
opts: Fetal yolk sac, fetal liver, and gastrointestinal tract
Placental syncytiotrophoblast
Maternal hepatocytes
Fetal adrenal cortex
questions.exp: AFP is a fetal-specific glycoprotein synthesized primarily by the secondary yolk sac in early gestation, and later by the fetal liver and GI tract. (Book p334)

questions.q: At what gestational age does fetal serum concentration of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) reach its maximal peak?
opts: 13 weeks of gestation
8 weeks of gestation
20 weeks of gestation
32 weeks of gestation
questions.exp: Fetal serum AFP levels peak at approximately 13 weeks of gestation, following which concentrations decline in fetal serum while rising in maternal serum. (Book p334)

questions.q: What is the optimal gestational age window for screening maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP)?
opts: 16 to 18 weeks of gestation (acceptable range: 15 to 20 weeks)
11 to 13 weeks + 6 days
24 to 28 weeks of gestation
6 to 8 weeks of gestation
questions.exp: MSAFP screening is ideally performed between 16 and 18 weeks (range 15-20 weeks); first-trimester MSAFP has very low diagnostic sensitivity. (Book p334)

questions.q: Which of the following conditions is characteristically associated with a pathologically ELEVATED maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP) level?
opts: Open neural tube defect (anencephaly, spina bifida aperta)
Down syndrome (Trisomy 21)
Complete hydatidiform mole
Overestimated gestational age
questions.exp: MSAFP is elevated in open NTDs, abdominal wall defects (gastroschisis, omphalocele), multiple pregnancy, fetal demise, and underestimated gestational age. (Book p334)

questions.q: Using the clinical mnemonic 'Diabetic GOAT', which of the following causes a DECREASE in maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP)?
opts: Maternal pregestational diabetes, Gestational trophoblastic disease, Overestimated dates, and Aneuploidy/Trisomies
Gastroschisis, Omphalocele, Anencephaly, and Twin gestation
Gestational diabetes, Oligohydramnios, Abruptio, and Teratoma
Glomerulonephritis, Open spina bifida, Atresia, and Turner syndrome
questions.exp: Decreased MSAFP ('Diabetic GOAT'): Diabetes, Gestational trophoblastic disease, Overestimated gestational age, Aneuploidy (Trisomy 21, 18, 13), Trisomies. (Book p334)

questions.q: What is the single most common chromosomal trisomy identified in first-trimester spontaneous miscarriages?
opts: Trisomy 16 (always lethal in embryogenesis)
Trisomy 21
Trisomy 18
Trisomy 13
questions.exp: Trisomy 16 is the single most common autosomal trisomy found in first-trimester spontaneous abortions; it is uniformly non-viable. (Book p335)

questions.q: What is the primary genetic mechanism responsible for approximately 95% of cases of Down syndrome (Trisomy 21)?
opts: Maternal meiotic non-disjunction (strongly linked to advanced maternal age)
Robertsonian translocation involving chromosomes 14 and 21
Mitotic non-disjunction producing mosaicism
Paternal meiotic deletion of the long arm of chromosome 21
questions.exp: 95% of Down syndrome cases arise from meiotic non-disjunction (overwhelmingly maternal Meiosis I), which correlates with maternal age. (Book p335)

questions.q: If a father or mother is an asymptomatic balanced carrier of a Robertsonian translocation between homologous chromosomes 21;21 [t(21q21q)], what is the chance of having a child with Down syndrome in every pregnancy?
opts: 100% chance
25% chance
50% chance
5-10% chance
questions.exp: A balanced homologous 21;21 translocation carrier can only produce gametes with either two 21s (Down) or zero 21s (monosomy 21, lethal), giving a 100% risk. (Book p335)

questions.q: In a family where a parent carries a balanced non-homologous Robertsonian translocation t(14;21), what is the empirical risk of Down syndrome in offspring when the MOTHER is the carrier versus when the FATHER is the carrier?
opts: 10-15% when mother is carrier; 2-5% when father is carrier
50% for mother; 50% for father
100% for mother; 0% for father
25% for mother; 10-15% for father
questions.exp: For balanced t(14;21) carriers, recurrence risk is 10-15% if the mother is the carrier, but only 2-5% if the father is the carrier. (Book p335)

questions.q: What is the gold standard diagnostic test to confirm fetal chromosomal aneuploidy when screening is positive?
opts: Karyotyping (G-banding) of fetal cells via CVS or amniocentesis
Targeted level II ultrasound
Cell-free fetal DNA quantification
Maternal serum triple test
questions.exp: Fetal karyotyping (or chromosomal microarray/FISH) obtained via invasive testing provides the definitive diagnostic confirmation of chromosomal abnormalities. (Book p336)

questions.q: What are the two maternal serum biochemical analytes measured in the first-trimester 'Dual test' between 11 and 13+6 weeks?
opts: Pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A) and free beta-hCG
Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and unconjugated estriol (uE3)
Inhibin-A and total hCG
Human placental lactogen (hPL) and progesterone
questions.exp: The Dual test measures serum PAPP-A and free beta-hCG between 11w0d and 13w6d (CRL 45-84 mm). (Book p336)

questions.q: In a fetus affected by Down syndrome (Trisomy 21), what typical pattern of PAPP-A and free beta-hCG is found on first-trimester biochemical screening?
opts: Decreased PAPP-A and increased free beta-hCG
Increased PAPP-A and decreased free beta-hCG
Both PAPP-A and free beta-hCG are markedly decreased
Both PAPP-A and free beta-hCG are markedly increased
questions.exp: Down syndrome displays reduced PAPP-A (<0.5 MoM) and elevated free beta-hCG (>2.0 MoM); in Trisomy 18 and 13, both analytes are significantly decreased. (Book p336)

questions.q: Beyond screening for chromosomal aneuploidies, an isolated finding of very low first-trimester maternal serum PAPP-A (<0.4 MoM) is an established predictor for:
opts: Placental insufficiency leading to fetal growth restriction (IUGR) and pre-eclampsia
Macrosomia and polyhydramnios
Gestational diabetes mellitus
Post-term prolonged pregnancy
questions.exp: Low first-trimester PAPP-A reflects impaired trophoblastic invasion and placentation, strongly predicting IUGR, pre-eclampsia, and preterm birth. (Book p336)

questions.q: What components constitute the 'Combined test' for first-trimester Down syndrome screening, and what is its approximate detection rate?
opts: Dual test (PAPP-A + free beta-hCG) plus sonographic Nuchal Translucency (NT); detection rate 82-87%
Triple test plus Level II targeted ultrasound; detection rate 65%
Nuchal translucency plus ductus venosus Doppler; detection rate 50%
Quad test plus NIPT; detection rate 70%
questions.exp: The first-trimester Combined test incorporates maternal age, Dual test analytes, and ultrasound NT, yielding an 82-87% detection rate for Down syndrome. (Book p336)

questions.q: Between what gestational age and CRL range must fetal Nuchal Translucency (NT) be measured?
opts: 11 weeks + 0 days to 13 weeks + 6 days (CRL 45 mm to 84 mm)
9 weeks + 0 days to 11 weeks + 0 days (CRL 25 mm to 44 mm)
14 weeks + 0 days to 16 weeks + 0 days (CRL 85 mm to 110 mm)
16 weeks + 0 days to 20 weeks + 0 days (CRL > 120 mm)
questions.exp: NT measurement is strictly validated between 11w0d and 13w6d when the embryonic CRL is 45 to 84 mm. (Book p337)

questions.q: What is the normal upper physiological cutoff for Nuchal Translucency (NT), above which it is classified as abnormally increased?
opts: < 3.0 mm (or < 95th percentile for CRL)
questions.exp: An NT measurement >= 3.0 mm (or >95th percentile) is pathologically thickened, signaling heightened risk of aneuploidy or structural heart disease. (Book p337)

questions.q: A thickened fetal Nuchal Translucency (>= 3.0 mm) with a normal fetal karyotype is an established indication to evaluate for which structural defect?
opts: Congenital heart disease (warrants specialized fetal echocardiography at 22-24 weeks)
Duodenal atresia
Polycystic kidney disease
Unilateral clubfoot
questions.exp: In chromosomally normal fetuses with elevated NT, major congenital cardiac defects are the most frequent structural anomaly, requiring fetal echo. (Book p337)

questions.q: What technical criteria must be fulfilled to obtain an accurate, standardized Nuchal Translucency (NT) measurement?
opts: Mid-sagittal plane, neutral fetal head (not flexed/extended), separate visualization of amnion, and calipers placed inner-to-inner
Transverse axial plane across the orbits with head fully extended
Coronal plane through the cervical spine with amnion touching the skin
Any plane showing the neck with calipers placed outer-to-outer
questions.exp: Standard NT criteria: mid-sagittal view, neutral head, magnification of head/thorax, separate amnion, and calipers placed inner-to-inner across widest lucency. (Book p337)

questions.q: How does a Cystic Hygroma differ sonographically and clinically from simple increased Nuchal Translucency?
opts: Cystic hygroma is a larger, widespread, multiseptated lymphatic sac extending beyond the neck, carrying higher aneuploidy risk
Cystic hygroma never contains internal septations and is limited to the subocciput
Cystic hygroma has no association with chromosomal abnormalities
Nuchal translucency always exhibits internal vascular flow on color Doppler
questions.exp: Cystic hygroma is a bilateral, multiseptated cystic lymphangioma extending along the posterolateral neck/body, carrying a >60% aneuploidy risk. (Book p338)

questions.q: Which biochemical analyte is added to the classic Triple test (AFP, hCG, uE3) to construct the Quadruple test for Down syndrome screening?
opts: Inhibin-A
Pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A)
Placental growth factor (PlGF)
Human placental lactogen (hPL)
questions.exp: The Quadruple test adds dimeric Inhibin-A to the Triple test, improving Down syndrome detection rate from ~70% to 80-83%. (Book p338)

questions.q: In a second-trimester quadruple test for Down syndrome, which two markers are elevated ('HI' is high)?
opts: hCG and Inhibin-A are elevated; AFP and uE3 are decreased
AFP and Inhibin-A are elevated; hCG and uE3 are decreased
uE3 and hCG are elevated; AFP and Inhibin-A are decreased
All four analytes are elevated
questions.exp: In Down syndrome, hCG and Inhibin-A ('HI') are abnormally high, while AFP and unconjugated estriol (uE3) are low. (Book p338)

questions.q: On second-trimester ultrasound (15-20 weeks), what cutoff for Nuchal Skinfold Thickness (NSFT) is considered an abnormal soft marker for Down syndrome?
questions.exp: In the second trimester (15-20 weeks), a nuchal fold thickness >=6 mm measured in the transcerebellar plane is a major soft marker for Down syndrome. (Book p338)

questions.q: Which of the following second-trimester sonographic soft tissue markers has the LOWEST individual risk of aneuploidy and is found in 11-17% of completely normal fetuses?
opts: Choroid Plexus Cyst (CPC)
Echogenic bowel
Absent nasal bone
Thickened nuchal skin fold
questions.exp: Choroid plexus cysts carry the lowest isolated risk for aneuploidy (found in 1-2% of normal fetuses, weak association with Trisomy 18); when isolated, normal outcome is expected. (Book p338)

questions.q: Non-Invasive Prenatal Testing (NIPT) analyzes cell-free fetal DNA (cffDNA) extracted from maternal blood. What is the tissue source of this cffDNA?
opts: Apoptosis of placental syncytiotrophoblast microvilli
Intact fetal red blood cells that crossed the placenta
Fetal leukocytes in maternal bone marrow
Amniotic fluid leaking into maternal capillaries
questions.exp: cffDNA in maternal plasma consists of short fragments (~150 bp) originating predominantly from apoptotic placental syncytiotrophoblast cells. (Book p339)

questions.q: From what gestational age onwards can Non-Invasive Prenatal Testing (NIPT) be reliably performed?
opts: >= 10 weeks of gestation (when fetal fraction is >= 4%)
>= 6 weeks of gestation
>= 16 weeks of gestation only
>= 20 weeks of gestation
questions.exp: NIPT can be performed from 10 weeks onward, when the placental cffDNA fraction consistently exceeds the minimum testing threshold of 4%. (Book p339)

questions.q: What is the primary clinical limitation of Non-Invasive Prenatal Testing (NIPT)?
opts: It is an advanced screening test, NOT a definitive diagnostic test; positive results must be confirmed invasively
It has a sensitivity of less than 70% for Down syndrome
It causes a 1% risk of miscarriage
It cannot be performed in Rh-negative mothers
questions.exp: Despite >99% sensitivity for Trisomy 21, NIPT is not diagnostic due to potential confined placental mosaicism; positive results mandate invasive confirmation. (Book p339)

questions.q: What is 'Integrated Screening' for Down syndrome, and what is its major ethical/clinical drawback?
opts: First-trimester (Dual + NT) and second-trimester (Quad) tests combined; results are withheld until second-trimester testing is completed
Sequential testing with immediate termination offered in the first trimester
Simultaneous NIPT and amniocentesis for all patients
Universal karyotyping in early pregnancy
questions.exp: Integrated screening combines 1st trimester Dual+NT with 2nd trimester Quad (detection rate 85-95%), but results are withheld until T2, delaying diagnosis. (Book p339)

questions.q: What is the standard clinical cutoff ratio used to define a 'screen-positive' result for Down syndrome (Trisomy 21)?
opts: 1 : 250 (e.g., 1:150 is screen-positive; 1:500 is screen-negative)
questions.exp: A risk greater than 1:250 (e.g., 1:100 or 1:200) is classified as screen-positive for Down syndrome, warranting invasive testing or NIPT. (Book p339)

questions.q: What is the standard screening cutoff ratio used to classify a pregnancy as high risk for Trisomy 18 (Edwards) and Trisomy 13 (Patau)?
questions.exp: For Trisomy 18 and Trisomy 13, the standard screen-positive cutoff ratio is typically set at 1:100. (Book p339)

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman receives a combined first-trimester screening report indicating a Down syndrome risk of 1:80. What is the most appropriate next step in clinical management?
opts: Offer diagnostic confirmation via Chorionic Villus Sampling (or amniocentesis) or secondary screening with NIPT
Reassure the patient that the fetus is entirely normal
Perform an immediate emergency Caesarean delivery
Repeat the same biochemical test next week
questions.exp: A risk of 1:80 is screen-positive (>1:250); genetic counseling should be provided, offering definitive invasive testing (CVS/amniocentesis) or NIPT. (Book p339)

questions.q: If a pregnant woman presents with positive first-trimester aneuploidy screening and chooses definitive invasive diagnostic testing, what procedure is performed at 11 to 13+6 weeks versus after 15 weeks?
opts: Chorionic Villus Sampling (CVS) in the first trimester; Amniocentesis after 15 weeks
Amniocentesis in the first trimester; CVS after 15 weeks
Cordocentesis at both gestational ages
Targeted ultrasound only at both gestational ages
questions.exp: Invasive diagnosis is achieved via CVS in the first trimester (10-14 weeks, ideally 11-13+6w) and via amniocentesis in the second trimester (15-20 weeks). (Book p339)
